title: Nervous and Endocrine Systems
seo_title: Year 9 Science: Nervous and Endocrine Systems Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Compare the role of body systems in regulating and coordinating the body's response to a stimulus, and describe the operation of a negative feedback mechanism (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 9 science worksheets on the nervous and endocrine systems: stimulus and response, neurons and reflex arcs, hormones, homeostasis and negative feedback for temperature and blood glucose. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Nerves are fast; hormones last longer.
key_sub: Negative feedback reverses a change to keep the body's conditions steady.
body_html:
How to think about it

Two systems coordinate the body's response to a stimulus.

  • Nervous system: receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord or brain → motor neuron → effector. Fast and short.
  • Endocrine system: glands release hormones into the blood. Slower but longer lasting (insulin, adrenaline).
  • Homeostasis uses negative feedback: a change is detected and reversed, such as sweating when too hot.
Example

Hand touches a hot pan. Order?

receptor in skin

sensory neuron

spinal cord

motor neuron

muscle

Answer: a reflex arc

Example

Blood glucose rises after lunch. Response?

pancreas releases insulin

Answer: glucose falls back to normal

Common mistakes

  • Thinking hormones act faster than nerves.
  • Thinking a reflex goes to the brain to decide first.
  • Thinking 'negative feedback' means something bad happens.

faq.q: What is the difference between the nervous and endocrine systems?
faq.a: The nervous system uses electrical impulses along neurons for fast, short responses. The endocrine system uses hormones in the blood for slower, longer lasting responses.
It is a control system that reverses a change. If body temperature rises, the body sweats and widens skin blood vessels to bring it back to about 37 °C.
Reflexes are fast, automatic responses that protect the body, such as blinking or pulling away from something hot.

items.q: Kai is learning about receptors. Which receptors respond to sweet and salty tastes?
items.e: Taste buds on the tongue respond to sweet and salty tastes and send messages to the brain.

items.q: Which hormone gets the body ready for 'fight or flight'?
items.e: It raises heart rate and breathing rate.

items.q: What carries messages through the nervous system?
items.e: Neurons carry electrical signals.

items.q: Priya is learning about receptors. Which receptors respond to balance and head motion?
items.e: Receptors in the inner ear respond to balance and head motion and send messages to the brain.

items.q: Amelia is learning about receptors. Which receptors respond to heat and cold?
items.e: Receptors in the skin respond to heat and cold and send messages to the brain.

items.q: Why is a reflex so fast?
c: the impulse goes through the spinal cord without waiting for the brain to decide
it goes to the brain twice
items.e: Reflexes protect the body.

items.q: Noah is learning about receptors. Which receptors respond to sound?
items.e: Receptors in the ears respond to sound and send messages to the brain.

items.q: Is the knee jerk when the tendon is tapped a reflex action or a voluntary action?
items.e: Reflexes are rapid, automatic and do not need conscious thought; voluntary actions are controlled by the brain consciously.

items.q: Jack notices a fire alarm and walks outside. Which shows the path of the message in order?
c: receptors → sensory nerves → brain → motor nerves → muscles
muscles → motor nerves → brain → sensory nerves → receptors
items.e: Stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → brain → motor neuron → muscle (response).

items.q: A cricket player at the Adelaide Oval sweats on a 40 °C day. How does sweating help?
c: Sweat adds water to the blood.
Sweat evaporates and takes heat away from the skin.
items.e: Evaporation cools the body.

items.q: Which system sends fast electrical messages along neurons?
items.e: Nerve impulses take milliseconds.

items.q: Which two parts make up the central nervous system?
c: the brain and the spinal cord
items.e: Nerves branch out from the spinal cord to the whole body.

items.q: Lachlan notices a buzzing bee and moves away. What is the response?
items.e: The response is what the body does after the brain processes the information.

items.q: Tom notices a red stop sign and stops the bike. Which shows the path of the message in order?
c: muscles → motor nerves → brain → sensory nerves → receptors
receptors → sensory nerves → brain → motor nerves → muscles
items.e: Stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → brain → motor neuron → muscle (response).

items.q: What is a stimulus?
c: a change in the environment that the body detects
items.e: A hot stove or a loud noise is a stimulus.

items.q: Is choosing a book to read a reflex action or a voluntary action?
items.e: Reflexes are rapid, automatic and do not need conscious thought; voluntary actions are controlled by the brain consciously.

items.q: Is pulling your hand away from a hot pan a reflex action or a voluntary action?
items.e: Reflexes are rapid, automatic and do not need conscious thought; voluntary actions are controlled by the brain consciously.

items.q: What can the brain do with information besides responding right away?
c: send it back to the eyes
items.e: Memories guide later behaviour.

items.q: Matilda is learning about receptors. Which receptors respond to pressure and touch?
items.e: Receptors in the skin respond to pressure and touch and send messages to the brain.

items.q: Priya notices a flash of lightning and goes indoors. Which part of the body decides how to respond?
items.e: Receptors detect; the brain processes and decides; muscles carry out the response.

items.q: What happens to blood vessels near the skin when you are too hot?
c: They narrow to keep heat in.
They widen so more heat is lost (vasodilation).
items.e: Red, flushed skin shows this.

items.q: When reading a book close up, what happens to the lens?
items.e: Near object: ciliary muscles contract, ligaments slacken, lens thicker. Bright light: circular muscles contract and the pupil becomes smaller.

items.q: Which term describes this: “a muscle or gland that carries out a response”?
items.e: An effector: a muscle or gland that carries out a response.

items.q: Compare nervous and hormonal control. For hormonal control, what is the speed?
items.e: Nervous: fast, electrical, short-lived, precise. Hormonal: slower, chemical in blood, longer-lasting, widespread.

items.q: What crosses a synapse?
c: a chemical that diffuses across the gap
items.e: The chemical triggers an impulse in the next neuron.

items.q: Compare nervous and hormonal control. For hormonal control, what is the duration of effect?
items.e: Nervous: fast, electrical, short-lived, precise. Hormonal: slower, chemical in blood, longer-lasting, widespread.

items.q: Which gland releases thyroxine?
items.e: The thyroid gland releases thyroxine into the blood.

items.q: Why are reflex actions fast?
c: They do not involve the conscious part of the brain.
They use the motor neuron only.
items.e: Automatic.

items.q: Which gland releases oestrogen and progesterone?
items.e: The ovaries releases oestrogen and progesterone into the blood.

items.q: Compare nervous and hormonal control. For nervous control, what is the duration of effect?
items.e: Nervous: fast, electrical, short-lived, precise. Hormonal: slower, chemical in blood, longer-lasting, widespread.

items.q: In type 1 diabetes, what does the pancreas fail to make?
items.e: People with type 1 diabetes inject insulin or use a pump.

items.q: What is homeostasis?
c: changing body temperature to match the air
items.e: Body temperature, blood glucose, water levels.

items.q: Which of these is released by the ovaries?
items.e: The ovaries releases oestrogen and progesterone into the blood.

items.q: Which of these is released by the thyroid gland?
items.e: The thyroid gland releases thyroxine into the blood.

items.q: Which gland releases insulin and glucagon?

items.e: Nervous: fast, electrical, short-lived, precise. Hormonal: slower, chemical in blood, longer-lasting, widespread.

items.e: Nervous: fast, electrical, short-lived, precise. Hormonal: slower, chemical in blood, longer-lasting, widespread.

items.q: What are the three parts of an automatic control system?
items.e: Receptors detect, coordination centres process, effectors respond.

items.q: What does negative feedback do?
c: reverses a change to bring a condition back to normal
only happens when you are sick
items.e: Negative does not mean bad.

items.q: Compare nervous and hormonal control. For hormonal control, what is the area affected?
items.e: Nervous: fast, electrical, short-lived, precise. Hormonal: slower, chemical in blood, longer-lasting, widespread.

items.q: Breathing faster when carbon dioxide rises is an example of which kind of feedback?

items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.e: Steady temperature, glucose, water.

items.q: Kai says, 'Hormones work faster than nerves.' Which evidence shows he is wrong?
c: Pulling your hand from a hot pan takes a fraction of a second, but growth hormone acts over years.
items.e: Nerves are fast; hormones are slower and longer lasting.

items.q: Which system sends chemical messages (hormones) in the blood?
items.e: Hormones are slower but last longer.

items.q: What does thyroxine control?
items.e: Controlled by negative feedback.

items.q: A runner forgets to drink water on a hot day. How do the kidneys respond?
c: They make less urine to save water.
items.e: Water balance.

items.q: A surf lifesaver on Bondi Beach has hot, red skin on a summer day. Which two responses are cooling him?
c: sweating and widening of skin blood vessels
items.e: Both release heat from the body.

items.q: A thermostat turns the heater off when a room is warm enough. How is this like the body?
c: Both use negative feedback to keep a set point.
items.e: Sensor, control, response.

items.q: What does adrenaline do?
c: increases the heart rate to prepare the body for 'fight or flight'
items.e: From the adrenal glands.

items.q: A graph shows blood glucose rising after breakfast and falling back within 2 hours. Which hormone causes the fall?

items.q: Zara drinks 1 L of water and collects her urine each hour. What pattern would she expect?
c: more urine for a few hours, then back to normal
items.e: The kidneys remove extra water by negative feedback.

items.q: A student exercises and measures heart rate every minute until it returns to resting. What is this investigating?
c: a feedback mechanism that restores homeostasis
items.e: Measure the return to normal.

items.q: Why is a fever followed by sweating when it breaks?

The body is making more heat.

items.e: Only the music should change.

items.q: Liam measures pulse rate before and after exercise. Why should he take readings until it is steady again?
c: to see how long negative feedback takes to return it to normal
items.e: Recovery time shows fitness.
